GUARDRAIL: influence/goodness is NOT truth — a faith can shape the world and still be false; stated plainly. Tom Holland = 'the historian' (NOT 'secular historian' [stale] and NOT 'apologist'). 'makes the case', never 'proves'.
voiceover: How much of the modern world is quietly downstream of Christianity? This section traces the fingerprints — including the ones sceptics rarely notice. A tiny, illegal sect became the faith of the Roman Empire — not by the sword, but while being persecuted for three centuries. The convictions that every human being has equal worth, and that the weak deserve protection, were not obvious to the ancient world. The historian Tom Holland traces them to a Christian revolution. The rise of modern science, the movement that abolished the slave trade, even the very idea that history can progress — each has deep Christian roots. None of this proves Christianity true — a faith can be enormously influential and still be false, and we say so plainly. Influence is not truth. Every one of these arguments gets a fully-cited deep-dive essay. Each claim is sourced, and the strongest objections are stated fairly, then answered. That is our standard — Checked Before Published. And you will not just read. On every essay an AI tutor answers your questions — ask it anything, or highlight a single sentence and ask about that exact line. Mastery mode lets you explain the argument back in your own words and have it graded. Daily practice brings the key points back just as you are about to forget them. There are pocket cards to share, and a Debate Arena to practise against an AI sceptic before the real conversation. Every essay comes in a plain-English version and a full deep dive, with read-aloud audio. What this section makes the case for is narrower, and harder to shrug off: that the moral world a sceptic takes for granted is more Christian than they know — reason enough to look again. Start anywhere, and follow it where it leads.
